title: 93% of Fund Managers Lose to the S&P 500. Here's Why
description:
S&P's SPIVA scorecard compares actively managed funds with their benchmark. Through June 30, 2026, 83% of US large-cap funds trailed the S&P 500 over 10 years, 90% over 15 years and 93% over 20 years. A big reason is cost: in 2025 the average actively managed fund charged about 0.57% a year versus 0.09% for broad index funds (asset-weighted).

Sources: S&P Dow Jones Indices, SPIVA U.S. Scorecard Mid-Year 2026, Report 1a (data to June 30, 2026); Morningstar 2026 US Fund Fee Study (May 2026, data to Dec 31, 2025). Past performance doesn't guarantee future results. Not financial advice.

scenes.say: Ninety-three percent of US large-cap fund managers trailed the S&P five hundred over the last twenty years.

visual.label: of large-cap funds trailed the S&P 500
visual.sub: 20 years to June 2026 · S&P SPIVA scorecard

scenes.say: That's from S&P's SPIVA scorecard. And it's not a fluke. Over ten years, eighty-three percent fell behind. Over fifteen, ninety percent.
Why? An S&P five hundred index fund simply holds the companies in the index. No stock picking, no star manager to pay.

In twenty twenty-five, active funds charged about zero point five seven percent a year on average. Broad index funds, about zero point zero nine. On ten thousand dollars, that's fifty-seven dollars versus nine, every year.
So to win, a manager must beat the market by more than their fee, year after year. Over decades, very few do.
